**On the Word "Still"**

There is a word I keep returning to, the way you might keep returning to a particular stone on a beach, turning it over, unsure what makes it different from the thousand others. The word is *still*. Five letters, one syllable, and yet it seems to contain more rooms than a house.

Start with the obvious sense: motionless. A still pond. A still morning before anyone is awake. This is the *still* of held breath, of a heron standing in shallows with its whole body organized around not moving. It is a physical word here, a word about bodies and surfaces and air. When we say the water is still, we mean that nothing is disturbing it, and also that it has become a kind of mirror, that stillness has made it capable of reflection. There is something almost moral in this—the suggestion that to be quiet is to be able to show what is around you.

But then there is the second sense, the one that has nothing to do with motion at all: *still* as in continuing. "Are you still there?" "I still think about it." Here the word has turned from space into time. It no longer describes a surface but a duration. Something has persisted past the point where it might reasonably have stopped. And often the persistence is a little surprising, or a little sad, or a little stubborn. *Still* in this sense carries the shadow of an expectation that things would have changed by now. She still lives in that house. He still writes letters by hand. The word admits that the world moved on and this one thing did not.

I find it beautiful that these two meanings share a body. Because they are, when you look closely, the same thing seen from two angles. The pond is still because it has not been disturbed; the feeling is still there because it has not been disturbed either. Both are about the absence of change. One absence happens across a surface, the other across years. The language, without anyone deciding it should, noticed that these were the same and gave them one word.

Then there is the third sense, which is quieter and lives mostly in particular phrases: *still* as in *nevertheless*. "It was raining. Still, we went." This is the *still* of persistence against resistance, and it is a cousin of the temporal sense but with a spine in it. It says: the facts were against us, and we continued. It is a small word that often sits at the beginning of a sentence like a person setting their jaw. I think of this as the most human of the three meanings, because it is the one that involves a choice. The pond does not choose to be still. The feeling does not choose to remain. But the person who says "still, we went" has weighed something and decided.

And then, off in a corner of the house, there is the noun. A still. The apparatus for distilling—for heating a liquid until it turns to vapor, then cooling the vapor until it turns back into liquid, purer than before. The word comes from *distill*, which comes from a Latin root meaning to drip down. This is the one that seems least related, and yet I cannot help noticing that a still works by a kind of stillness. The vapor rises, gathers, and in the cold coil it slows, condenses, drops. Something rushing becomes something quiet and concentrated. What was diffuse becomes essence. If you wanted a metaphor for what attention does, you could do worse than a copper still in a shed somewhere, patiently turning heat into clarity.

There is also the photographic *still*: a single frame lifted out of a moving picture. Here the word has become a noun again, and it means something like "a moment held." A film runs at twenty-four frames per second, and each frame is, technically, a still—an instant in which nothing moves because time has been sliced too thin for movement to occur. When you pull one out and print it, you are performing a small act of rescue. You are saying: this, this one, is worth stopping for. Out of the river of images, this one stone.

I like that all of these uses seem to circle a single idea without ever quite landing on it. The idea is something like: *what remains when motion is subtracted*. The pond when the wind stops. The love when the years pass. The resolve when the reasons fail. The essence when the vapor cools. The frame when the film halts. Each is a kind of residue, a kind of what-is-left. And what is left, in each case, turns out to be the thing itself, seen more clearly than it could be seen while everything was moving.

Maybe this is why the word calms me. Most words for quietness are a little negative—*silence* is the absence of sound, *calm* is the absence of storm, *peace* is the absence of war. But *still* does not feel like an absence. It feels like a presence that was there all along and has finally become visible. The still pond is not empty; it is full of sky. The feeling that is still there is not a failure to move on; it is proof that something was real enough to stay.

I have no conclusion, really, except a small one: that a language is a record of what people noticed, and that someone, or many someones across many centuries, noticed that quietness and persistence and purity and the held moment all had something in common, and let them share a word. We inherited that noticing. We use it a dozen times a day without thinking. But every now and then it is worth stopping—being still, for a second—to see how much a single syllable can carry, and how patiently it has been carrying it.
